question: Do apparently flat finite-norm endpoints of MLP training conceal asymptotic descent channels created by neuron-duplication symmetry, and what function and optimizer dynamics emerge as paired input weights coalesce while opposite readout weights diverge?

key_findings.claim: Neuron duplication embeds every critical point of an r-neuron network into an equal-loss line of critical points in an r+1-neuron network, but stable finite segments are a fragile special case.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 2 duplicates one input vector and splits its output weight with parameter gamma. In bias-free scalar-output 2D regression, 10-30% of random initializations reach duplicated-neuron plateau saddles for the displayed widths; adding biases nearly eliminates exact stable duplicate solutions, consistent with stricter multi-output/deep stability conditions.

anchors.section: 2 Neuron duplication introduces lines of critical points

key_findings.claim: The proposed channel signature combines divergent opposite-signed readout weights, convergent input vectors, and late updates parallel to a symmetry-induced saddle direction.
key_findings.evidence: Gradient-flow trajectories perturbed from a saddle line enter an extremely slow descending path in which |a_i|+|a_j| grows without bound, cosine distance between w_i and w_j tends to zero, and parameter updates align with the saddle-line direction. A two-dimensional loss slice can falsely suggest two channels, while full gradient trajectories show only one side is attractive.

anchors.section: 3 Seemingly flat regions as channels to infinity

key_findings.claim: The empirical occurrence study is extensive for small smooth MLP regressors but operationally defines infinity by thresholds and a norm-censoring regularizer.
key_findings.evidence: The authors train 4,420 networks across modified Rosenbrock and four Matérn-3/2 Gaussian-process targets, input dimensions and widths 2-16, one to three hidden layers, softplus/erf activations, and 50 initializations per configuration. A channel requires parameter norm above 1,000, input cosine distance below 1e-3, and over 90% of updates in the proposed channel subspace; the ODE solver activates a cubic regularizer at maxnorm and stops trajectories classified as infinite.

key_findings.claim: Channels are common in every tested regression family and more frequent for rougher GP targets, but the paper does not report uncertainty for occurrence probabilities or establish target roughness as causal.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4c reports substantial channel probability across datasets and architectures and a positive trend with the GP kernel scale s; every GP target is redrawn by configuration and only 50 fits are run per cell. Target family, input dimension, width, and activation change together across aggregations, and there is no intervention holding function values or derivative demand fixed while varying roughness alone.

key_findings.claim: Finite-norm and channel endpoints have similar training-loss distributions, while channel trajectories simultaneously become flatter along the divergent direction and sharper orthogonally.
key_findings.evidence: Across the GP s=0.5 experiments, no evident loss separation appears between classified endpoints. Minimum Hessian magnitude stays extremely small along the channel while the largest eigenvalue rises; the explicit landscape slice shows narrowing in the maximum-curvature direction as gamma grows.

key_findings.claim: The functional limit of a two-neuron channel is a neuron plus a gated directional derivative, derived from a central finite difference rather than learned as an explicit GLU architecture.
key_findings.evidence: With midpoint w, separation epsilon, direction Delta, finite sum c, and scaled difference a=epsilon(a_i-a_j), Equation 4 gives c sigma(w·x)+a(Delta·x)sigma'(w·x) as epsilon tends to zero. For softplus, sigma' is sigmoid, producing a GLU-like term; readout difference grows as 1/epsilon and input distance shrinks as epsilon.

anchors.section: 4 Channels converge to gated linear units
C.2 Expansion of the loss in epsilon
C.6.1 First derivative with two neurons

key_findings.claim: Asymptotic scaling along one selected channel matches the finite-difference theory, but the evidence uses an artificial jump procedure and is not a general convergence proof.
key_findings.evidence: The procedure repeatedly halves epsilon at fixed reparameterized coordinates and briefly reintegrates gradient flow. In one 81-parameter, eight-input, eight-hidden-softplus Rosenbrock fit, loss and approximation error decay as epsilon squared, sharpness grows as 1/epsilon squared, and c, a, w, and Delta stabilize. The authors explicitly state that general convergence is difficult and use this acceleration because ordinary ODE trajectories reach only inverse epsilon of a few hundred.

key_findings.claim: A four-parameter population-loss toy supplies an actual stable optimum at infinity and explains why finite-step optimizers stop at an apparent finite solution.
key_findings.evidence: Two bias-free erf neurons fit a one-dimensional teacher whose central wiggle benefits from an erf derivative. Analytical population integrals yield two stable epsilon=0 channel minima and a plateau saddle; SGD and Adam reach channel entrances but stop where Hessian sharpness approaches 2/eta. Because lambda_max scales as 1/epsilon squared, finite step size imposes epsilon_min proportional to sqrt(eta).

anchors.section: Population-loss toy and edge of stability

key_findings.claim: The deep- and multi-neuron extensions are empirical or formal constructions rather than a characterization of practical network channels.
key_findings.evidence: Channels appear in any or several layers of small three-hidden-layer MLPs, and clusters of three or more near-equal input weights suggest multidimensional channels. Appendix C constructs a hierarchy in which r neurons and readout divergences of different orders yield higher derivatives, but the paper does not show which higher-order units are reached, stable, or useful in trained large networks.

anchors.section: C.6.2 Second derivative with three neurons

key_findings.claim: Claims of generic relevance to Transformers, CNNs, model fusion, robustness, continual learning, and generalization remain hypotheses outside the evaluated evidence.
key_findings.evidence: All occurrence experiments are small supervised regressions with smooth MLPs; a constructed infinite-data ReLU example only shows possibility. The discussion explicitly says quantifying channels in large Transformer and convolutional networks is ongoing, reports no test loss or downstream benefit, and offers no evidence for the proposed applications.

method.core_idea: Start from neuron-duplication symmetries, follow high-precision gradient-flow trajectories near the resulting saddle lines, operationally detect paths with coalescing input weights and diverging opposite readouts, and reparameterize paired neurons to identify the limiting function.
method.mechanism: Escaping an unstable duplication saddle can place optimization in a valley asymptotically parallel to the output-weight splitting direction. As the pair's input displacement epsilon shrinks and readout difference grows as 1/epsilon, their finite difference approaches a directional derivative of the activation, adding a gated linear unit. The same scaling makes the channel slope vanish as epsilon cubed while orthogonal sharpness diverges as 1/epsilon squared, so finite-step optimizers stop near the edge of stability and appear to have reached a flat finite minimum.
assumptions: The key derivation uses differentiable smooth activations and paired neurons in a fully connected layer.
The main theoretical setup is a one-hidden-layer scalar-output network with mean-squared error; extensions rely on the local pair interaction.
Gradient-flow ODE integration faithfully exposes asymptotic geometry that practical discrete optimizers approach only partially.
Channel classification thresholds at norm 1,000, cosine distance 1e-3, and 90% projected updates distinguish channels from other divergent trajectories.
A maxnorm regularizer and stopping rule do not qualitatively create the classified unbounded behavior.
For the general expansion, limiting coordinates c, a, w, and Delta exist and the epsilon-squared correction has the stabilizing sign.
The population-loss toy assumes standard Gaussian inputs and a teacher amenable to analytic erf integrals.
The edge-of-stability estimate uses a local Hessian scaling argument and fixed-step gradient descent intuition.

techniques.role: Creates symmetry-induced equal-loss saddle lines from narrower-network critical points.
Perturbs along the most negative Hessian eigenvector and follows full-dimensional ODE trajectories.
Combines norm, input-cosine, and projected-update criteria to classify empirical endpoints.
Expresses paired neurons through midpoint, separation, direction, sum, and scaled readout difference.
Artificially halves separation and relaxes remaining coordinates to probe asymptotic scaling.
Uses Gaussian integrals to establish stable finite and infinite critical points in a four-parameter toy.
Shows concurrent flattening along the channel and sharpening in transverse directions.
Constructs multi-neuron limits that can express first and higher activation derivatives.

evaluations.setting: Bias-free two-dimensional modified-Rosenbrock regression with one-hidden-layer scalar MLPs of widths 1-5
evaluations.metric: Unique minima, duplicated-neuron frequency, gradient norm, Hessian signs, and perturbation trajectories
evaluations.result: Stable plateau-saddle segments occur in roughly 10-30% of runs for shown widths but mostly vanish after adding bias
evaluations.baseline: Same architectures with versus without bias and neighboring unstable gamma segments

evaluations.setting: 4,420 softplus/erf MLP regressions across Rosenbrock and four GP roughness scales, dimensions/widths 2-16, and one to three hidden layers
evaluations.metric: Thresholded channel frequency, training loss, Hessian extrema, layer location, and channel dimensionality
evaluations.result: Classified channels appear in all tested families, increase with target roughness, have similar loss to finite endpoints, and become flatter and sharper
evaluations.baseline: Finite-norm local minima found under the same ODE protocol

evaluations.setting: One selected 81-parameter softplus network followed by the jump procedure
evaluations.metric: Loss, GLU approximation error, limiting coordinates, cosine geometry, and largest Hessian eigenvalue versus epsilon
evaluations.result: Observed epsilon-squared loss/error decay and inverse-epsilon-squared sharpness match the asymptotic expansion
evaluations.baseline: The predicted scaling laws; no independent network sample or natural unaccelerated endpoint at extreme epsilon

evaluations.setting: Two-neuron, bias-free erf population regression with a one-dimensional Gaussian input
evaluations.metric: Analytical loss landscape, epsilon stability coefficient, gradient-flow trajectories, and SGD/Adam endpoint versus step size
evaluations.result: One channel is the best stable solution at infinity while finite-step methods stop at the predicted edge-of-stability boundary
evaluations.baseline: Plateau saddle, second higher-loss channel, and finite-data gradient flow

evaluations.metric: Approximation of a target exactly representable as a ReLU gated directional derivative
evaluations.result: Demonstrates that a ReLU channel is possible when finite-data cusp effects are removed
evaluations.baseline: Existence construction only, not an occurrence or optimization-frequency study

limitations: Empirical evidence is confined to small MLP regression; no Transformer, CNN, classification, generative, or modern large-scale training run is measured.
Unboundedness is inferred from finite threshold crossing plus asymptotic theory, not observed at literal infinity.
The ODE protocol uses a maxnorm-dependent cubic regularizer and stopping rule that require sensitivity checks beyond those shown.
Channel frequencies depend on hand-set norm, cosine-distance, and update-projection thresholds and are reported without confidence intervals.
The jump procedure is not natural optimizer dynamics and is demonstrated on one selected network.
The general GLU limit is algebraic; stability requires the limiting coordinates to converge and the epsilon-squared loss coefficient to be positive.
Finding the saddle line corresponding to a naturally discovered channel remains an explicit open heuristic problem.
No held-out generalization, robustness, calibration, or downstream value is compared between channel and finite-norm solutions.
Weight decay and finite step size can stop divergence, so the literal infinite limit may be irrelevant to standard practical training while the approximate GLU still appears.
Higher-dimensional channels and higher derivatives are not empirically characterized for stability or utility.
failure_modes: Large opposing readouts can cancel numerically, producing overflow or loss of precision before reaching a useful finite-difference regime.
Cosine-near input weights may be collinear at different norms rather than close in Euclidean space, invalidating the midpoint expansion assumed by the detector.
A high-norm divergent trajectory can satisfy threshold criteria transiently without converging to stable limiting coordinates.
Finite data with ReLU can introduce cusps that trap dynamics for reasons unrelated to an asymptotic channel.
Weight decay can select a finite biased approximation and prevent the best unregularized GLU limit.
Finite-step EoS oscillations can make a channel look like a stationary flat minimum under ordinary stopping criteria.
Multiple neuron groups and overlapping channels can make pairwise attribution non-identifiable.
The heuristic reverse map from channel to saddle line can merge the wrong neurons or relax to another channel.
A channel can achieve training loss comparable to finite minima without improving test behavior or functional simplicity.
reusable_insights: Audit apparently converged flat solutions for coordinated weight divergence and function-space convergence before declaring a finite local minimum.
Track sharpness and flatness in separate directions; a single scalar sharpness summary can conceal a narrowing transverse valley with an extremely flat tangent.
Reparameterize canceling units into finite sums and scaled differences to reveal stable function-space coordinates.
Distinguish parameter divergence from functional divergence: opposite large weights may converge to a bounded derivative feature.
Report threshold sensitivity and censoring rules whenever classifying minima at infinity numerically.
Compare natural optimizer time with accelerated continuation procedures; the latter characterize geometry but not reachability.
Finite step size and regularization act as implicit cutoffs on asymptotic representational mechanisms.
Use explicit matched gated architectures to test whether emergent channel formation signals an architectural mismatch.
open_questions: How often do channel signatures occur inside Transformer MLPs, convolutional channels, and large-scale classification networks under standard training?
Can a prospective detector distinguish a true asymptotic channel from transient large-weight cancellation before an arbitrary norm threshold?
Do channel-derived GLUs improve held-out loss, robustness, calibration, or transfer relative to finite-norm minima at equal compute?
Can one prove generic convergence and full Hessian stability at the limiting GLU rather than only an epsilon expansion?
What optimizer, weight-decay, precision, and batch-noise regimes enter or avoid channels?
Can the nearest generating saddle manifold be recovered uniquely from a trained channel solution?
Which higher-order derivative units are dynamically reachable with three or more neurons, and are they stable?
Would replacing smooth neuron pairs with explicit GLUs remove channel formation and improve conditioning without sacrificing function quality?

competitive_landscape.title: Embedding Principle: a hierarchical structure of loss landscape of deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. prove that narrower-network critical points embed into wider networks and characterize Hessian inertia monotonicity. The target paper starts from this hierarchy but follows nearby escaping trajectories to a new asymptotic function-space limit rather than classifying embedded critical manifolds alone.

competitive_landscape.title: The loss landscape of overparameterized neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Cooper proves that overparameterized global minima generically form high-dimensional finite manifolds. The target paper studies slow decreasing paths whose parameter norm diverges and whose endpoint is a local function-space minimum at infinity, a different source of apparent flatness.

competitive_landscape.title: Steepest Descent Neural Architecture Optimization: Escaping Local Optimum with Signed Neural Splitting
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. deliberately add signed neuron copies to escape splitting-stable local optima and grow architectures on practical vision benchmarks. The target paper passively analyzes naturally reached paired-neuron channels and their GLU limit, without proposing architecture growth or benchmarking task performance.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen et al. establish the generic empirical regime where lambda_max hovers near 2/eta and loss oscillates. The target paper identifies a specific asymptotic valley whose inverse-epsilon-squared sharpening predicts where EoS truncates approach to a GLU minimum.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen et al. show adaptive optimizers equilibrate a preconditioned Hessian at an adaptive stability threshold and can enter higher-curvature regions. The target paper shows Adam stopping early in one four-parameter channel but does not analyze preconditioned curvature or explain adaptive motion in general channels.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploring Neural Network Landscapes: Star-Shaped and Geodesic Connectivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Lin, Li, and Wu prove and observe low-barrier finite paths and star-shaped connectivity among minima. The target paper studies a one-sided path of monotonically decreasing loss toward infinite norm, emphasizing local symmetry alignment and functional derivatives rather than connectivity among trained endpoints.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Modeling with Gated Convolutional Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Dauphin et al. introduce explicit GLUs and demonstrate language-model gains and latency benefits. The target paper derives a GLU-like directional derivative as the infinite-weight limit of two smooth neurons, but does not compare its emergent approximation with an explicit GLU at matched capacity or optimization cost.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Optimization in Deep Learning with Central Flows
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen et al. derive central flows that predict smoothed optimizer trajectories in oscillatory EoS regimes for generic networks. The target paper uses exact ODE flow plus a local 2/eta cutoff argument; a central-flow analysis could test whether discrete optimizers actually progress along, leave, or orbit its channels.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Neural loss landscapes generically contain extremely flat channels to local minima at infinity, asymptotically parallel to neuron-duplication saddle lines, and paired neurons at their ends implement gated linear units; standard optimizers reach these channels frequently but appear to stop at finite flat minima.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines symmetry geometry, 4,420 high-precision small-network runs, a paired-neuron finite-difference limit, asymptotic scaling under continuation, a population-loss existence example, and a finite-step EoS cutoff.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest distinct contribution is the coherent geometry-to-function account linking duplicate-neuron symmetry, a slow infinite-norm valley, and an emergent gated derivative. The result is convincing as an existence and small-MLP phenomenon, not yet generic for modern networks or beneficial for generalization. Research on detecting and exploiting the channels would substantially overlap existing symmetry-breaking, activation-basis, and curvature-clamped EoS flagships unless it introduces a genuinely new function-space identifiability target and large-model intervention.
